extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary travel essays; aspiring travel/travelogue writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing literary travel essays and creative non‑fiction that mix personal anecdote, vivid local description, historical context, and moral reflection without sensationalism or prurience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and verification in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat or publish sensational, unverified stories or myths about events or people; verify facts with people on the spot or reliable authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes syndicated foreign correspondence that prints "colossal winnings of purely imaginary players," noting people on the spot know such stories did not happen: "People upon the spot know that nothing of the kind happened, and that no person of that name had appeared upon the scene. The story on the face of it bears to the knowing its own refutation." He commends prudent attribution (e.g., ascribing rumor to 'the head croupier') only when necessary, and urges skepticism toward hearsay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism and fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the temptation to dramatize or fabricate to make copy more exciting; do not invent characters or improbably large, lurid outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lampoons "space-writers" and press reports that invent grand gambling exploits and implies that cheap gambling stories proliferate when news is scarce. Example criticisms include the fanciful accounts of Mr. Darnbrough and the inflated accounts of 'Wells'—used as anti‑patterns of what not to print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prurient or salacious detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include lurid, prurient material for its own sake; prefer tasteful, humane treatment of personal tragedies and scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly states: "it will contain not a line to feed any prurient fancy," arguing instead for records of ordinary journeys (e.g., between the coiffeur and the flower market) rather than salacious anecdotes. He recounts the tragic story of a fallen woman with restraint as an example of how to treat painful subjects without exploiting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal anecdote and intimate detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor the narrative in personal experience and well‑chosen anecdotes to give immediacy, authority, and charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay is built from first‑hand vignettes—acquaintance with the man 'who broke the bank,' meetings with Leopold II, tales of living in a Paris pension, and the Mr. Barnes tipping story—demonstrating that well‑placed anecdotes provide color and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid descriptive comparison and local color
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete images, comparisons, and sensory detail to evoke place and climate; use analogies to familiar locales when helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing the Riviera climate to Southern Florida; describing Monte Carlo's setting "nestled under the heights of La Condamine and Tête de Chien"; praising Charles Garnier's Casino as one of the most beautiful buildings. Such particulars and analogies help readers visualize and feel the locale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide historical and contextual background
rubrics_metrics.description: Enrich travel/essay writing with historical facts and institutional context that illuminate why a place is the way it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author situates the Corniche Road as built by the First Napoleon, explains Monte Carlo's commercial/political origins (the Grimaldi bargain with an Alsatian gambler), and recounts institutional details (Monaco's coins, police, treaty relationships) to deepen the reader's understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced, fair characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray people (including controversial figures) with nuance; avoid repeating calumny and seek to understand motives and businesslike causes rather than caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In defending Leopold II against simplistic portrayals as a 'sot' and a 'roué,' the author emphasizes his businesslike nature and warns against the unbalanced attack of commercial and humanitarian critics, illustrating the value of measured, evidence‑based character sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint about controversy; prefer tasteful prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise restraint when entering contentious topics; if the writer dislikes controversy, treat debatable subjects cautiously and avoid gratuitous provocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer avers: "if there is anything in this world that I do hybominate, it is controversy!" and elsewhere avoids sensational gossip—advising a temperate, non‑combative tone when touching on fraught matters (e.g., social scandals, political accusations).
